# Abstract 30
- Self-supervised  denoising  methods  significantly  enhance  the  signal-to-noise  ratio  in 31 fluorescence  neural  imaging,  yet  real-time  solutions  remain  scarce  in  high-speed 32 applications. Here, we present the FrAme-multiplexed SpatioTemporal learning strategy 33 (FAST), a deep-learning framework designed for high-speed fluorescence neural imaging, 34 including  in  vivo  calcium,  voltage,  and  volumetric  time-lapse  imaging.  FAST  balances 35 spatial and temporal redundancy across neighboring pixels, preserving structural fidelity 36 while  preventing  over-smoothing  of  rapidly  evolving  fluorescence  signals.  Utilizing  an 37 ultra-light  convolutional neural network, FAST enables real-time processing at speeds 38 exceeding  1,000  frames  per  second.  We  also  introduce  an  intuitive  graphical  user 39 interface (GUI) that integrates FAST into standard imaging workflows, providing a real40 time  denoising  tool  for  recorded  neural  activity  and  enabling  downstream  analysis  in 41 neuroscience research that requires millisecond-scale temporal precision, particularly in 42 closed-loop studies. 43

# Introduction 44
Intravital  neural  imaging  is  critical  for  understanding  brain  science,  especially  in 45 examining  neural  circuit  dynamics  underlying  behavioral  paradigms  and  investigating 46 disease-specific mechanisms such as neurodegeneration and epilepsy 1 -5 . Fluorescence 47 imaging, an essential technique in neuroscience to characterize  neural structures and 48 activities, is currently facing technical ceilings due to the limitations in fluorescent probes 49 and light scattering in deep brain tissues 6 -9 . Increases in imaging depth and speed often 50 come at the expense of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), posing challenges for high-quality 51 data acquisition. Recent advances in denoising methods aim to address these issues 10 -52 14 , yet different imaging scenarios demand tailored denoising solutions 14 -17 . For example, 53 structural  imaging  emphasizes  preserving  high  spatial  resolution 18 -21 ,  while  functional 54 imaging  prioritizes  high  temporal  resolution 13 -16 .  Furthermore,  in  closed-loop  neural 55 modulation, the process must seamlessly integrate imaging, analysis, and stimulation 22 , 56 adding further complexity to the already demanding requirements for high-speed, high57 SNR imaging. Therefore,  an  ideal  denoising  tool  that  is  universally  applicable  across 58 different imaging scenarios and enables real-time feedback remains highly desired but is 59 still  lacking,  particularly  in  ultra-high-speed  neural  activity  recording  at  the  millisecond 60 scale. 61

# Real-time enhancement in high-speed voltage imaging with FAST. 258
Voltage imaging is a powerful technique for monitoring rapid neuronal activity, capable of 259 resolving millisecond-scale changes in membrane potential with high temporal precision. 260 Unlike calcium imaging, which reflects indirect activity signals, voltage imaging provides 261 a direct and precise representation of electrophysiological events. Recent advances in 262 voltage indicators, such as QuasAr6a 37  and zArchon1 38 , have significantly contributed to 263 enabling imaging speeds up to 1,000 Hz, allowing researchers to resolve fast voltage 264 transients critical for understanding neural dynamics. However, such high-speed imaging 265 significantly reduces photon collection, leading to a low SNR. The resulting noise not only 266

- obscures neuronal morphology but also distorts voltage signals, making it challenging to 267 extract meaningful dynamics. These challenges necessitate robust denoising methods 268 that can preserve both the spatial and temporal fidelity of voltage imaging data. Here, we 269 demonstrate that FAST effectively addresses these challenges by removing noise while 270 faithfully  preserving  voltage  transients.  We  evaluated  FAST's  performance  through 271 simulation  experiments, in  vivo single-neuron  imaging  in  the  mouse  cortex,  and 272 population-level  imaging  in  the  zebrafish  spinal  cord.  Our  results  show  that  FAST 273 significantly improves both the clarity of neuronal morphology and the fidelity of extracted 274 voltage signals, enabling more accurate analysis of neural activity under extreme imaging 275 conditions. 276

# Discussion 452
Noise presents a significant challenge in intravital neural observation, with inherent shot 453 noise  setting  the  ceiling  for  the  SNR  in  fluorescence  imaging,  thereby  constraining 454 resolution,  speed,  and  sensitivity.  Effective  denoising  is  crucial,  and  different  imaging 455 scenarios  require  tailored  approaches:  structural  imaging  benefits  from  high  spatial 456 resolution, while functional imaging demands high temporal resolution. Self-supervised 457 deep learning methods have emerged as powerful tools for denoising, and leveraging 458 spatiotemporal  redundancy  in  raw  data.  However,  existing  approaches  often  involve 459 complex training and resource-intensive processes, and it remains challenging to provide 460 the fast, high-quality denoising techniques needed for neuroscience research to support 461 real-time  data  analysis  and  closed-loop  neural  modulation.  We  introduce  FAST,  a 462 universal real-time self-supervised denoising pipeline for diverse neural  imaging 463 scenarios. FAST uses a lightweight 2D convolutional network to balance temporal and 464 spatial redundancies, achieving rapid denoising speeds beyond 1,000 FPS, and extreme 465 to  2,100  FPS.  It  has  been  validated  across  various  imaging  scenarios  and  subjects, 466

- demonstrating superior denoising performance and real-time capability. FAST enhances 467 cellular morphology restoration, neuron segmentation, and 3D calcium event extraction 468 while preserving  spike  shapes  and  improving  voltage  transient  correlations  with 469 electrophysiological  recordings.  A  user-friendly  GUI  further  facilitates  training,  offline 470 inference, and real-time online inference, enabling state-of-the-art denoising of user data. 471

Previous denoising methods for fluorescence time-lapse imaging often relied on large472 scale network structures, such as 3D  convolutional networks, Transformers, or 473 combinations of multiple architectures 15,16,21,24 . However, we argue that such complexity 474 is  unnecessary.  FAST,  with  its  spatiotemporal  balanced  training  strategy,  achieves 475 denoising speeds exceeding 1,000 FPS on a single GPU using only a lightweight 2D 476 convolutional network. The performance of FAST meets the real-time denoising demands 477 of most imaging systems, while still leaving time windows available for additional post478 processing operations, such as cluster analysis of large-scale neuronal imaging, real479 time spike inference, functional connectivity analysis, online activity pattern recognition, 480 optogenetic stimulation feedback, and automated ROI selection and tracking 44 -48 . 481

Existing self-supervised time-lapse denoising methods rely on temporal redundancy to 482 recover true signals from noisy data. These methods are based on the assumption that 483 information  carriers  maintain  ergodicity  across  adjacent  temporal  coordinates.  This 484 foundational  assumption,  however,  confronts  inherent  limitations  when  the  temporal 485 sampling rate is low or the signal's dynamics are fast. Hence, in practical ultra -high speed 486 imaging acquisition, such as neuronal voltage imaging, the dynamics between a spike 487 window are too sharp to maintain the assumption after temporal subsampling, and further 488 lead deviations that can lead to distortion and smoothed spatial structure of recovered 489 signals.  Most  current  methods  seek  to  maximize  the  temporal  input  range,  aiming  to 490 enhance denoising performance by capturing potential signal features. However, a wider 491 temporal input range often contains several dynamics. A self-supervised approach relying 492 solely on temporal redundancy would cause a phantasm of temporal causality, wherein 493 signal  restoration  highly  depends  on  future  signals,  especially  in  3D  convolutional 494 networks. This temporal causality phantasm inevitably introduces uncertainties in ultra495 high speed imaging, compromising the authenticity of the restored signal. FAST mitigates 496

- this issue by incorporating adjustable trade-off parameters that constrain the temporal 497 receptive field and expand the spatial receptive field. By tuning the information-receiving 498 range, FAST effectively minimizes interference at its source, preserving the authenticity 499 of neural signals while reducing noise. This controlled approach enables the rapid and 500 faithful  restoration  of  high-fidelity  signals  without  relying  on  extensive  spatiotemporal 501 inputs. 502

Our well-designed frame-multiplexed spatiotemporal learning strategy equips FAST with 503 a universal self-supervised denoising capability, demonstrated to be effective across a 504 wide  range  of  biological  samples,  including  zebrafish  and  mice.  It  is  versatile  in  its 505 application,  supporting  multiple  imaging  modalities  such  as  calcium  imaging,  voltage 506 imaging, and volumetric imaging, as well as various imaging techniques like confocal 507 microscopy,  light-sheet  microscopy,  and  multi-photon  microscopy.  Beyond  this,  we 508 believe FAST has the potential to be implemented in other biomedical optical imaging 509 techniques,  offering  improvements  in  depth,  resolution,  and  speed.  Therefore,  we 510 envision FAST as providing universal ultra-fast denoising integrated with imaging systems 511 and experimental requirements, thereby opening up new possibilities for advanced and 512 verifiable biomedical research. 513

# Network architecture and loss function 535
Network structure: The FAST network is a meticulously designed ultra-lightweight 2D 536 U-Net, as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 3.  Similar to the original U-Net 48 , our network 537 architecture employs an encoder-decoder structure with skip connections.  In our network, 538 we use two encoding blocks to reduce the dimensionality.  Each encoding block consists 539 of a 3×3 group convolutional layer (with each group processing 2 channels) followed by 540 a BatchNorm layer, a ReLU activation, and a 3×3 max-pooling layer.  To restore the input 541 dimensions, we  use two decoding blocks, each containing a nearest-neighbor 542 interpolation, followed by a 3×3 group convolutional layer (with each group processing 2 543 channels), a BatchNorm layer, and a ReLU activation.  Group convolutions reduce the 544 number  of  parameters  and  computational  cost  while  enabling  independent  feature 545 extraction  within  each  group,  which  helps  mitigate  interference  between  groups  and 546 avoids artifacts caused by temporal signal aliasing.  At each resolution depth, the number 547 of channels in each feature map is 64.  We employ skip connections to connect the output 548 of the second encoding block to the input of the corresponding decoding block. 549

Compared to the original U-Net, we have made two principal modifications.  First, we 550 reduced  the  number  of  downsampling  steps  to  two.  Downsampling  increases  the 551 receptive field, allowing the convolutional kernels to extract features over a larger image 552 area.  However, as the number of downsampling steps increases, so does the number of 553 network parameters.  Our spatial subsampler can be regarded as a single downsampling 554

- step  that  expands  the  receptive  field,  thereby  allowing  us  to  reduce  the  number  of 555
- downsampling steps in the U-Net to shrink the network.  Second, we eliminated the top556

level skip connection.  Skip connections can fuse low-level and high-level features, but in

denoising  tasks,  high-level  features  are  often  noise  that  needs  to  be  suppressed.

Therefore, removing the top-level skip connection can improve denoising performance.

- By  minimizing  the  network  depth,  the  number  of  channels  per  feature  map,  and  the 560 number of skip connections, our network trains with only approximately 0.13M parameters. 561

# Real-time enhancement in high-speed voltage imaging with FAST. 258
Voltage imaging is a powerful technique for monitoring rapid neuronal activity, capable of 259 resolving millisecond-scale changes in membrane potential with high temporal precision. 260 Unlike calcium imaging, which reflects indirect activity signals, voltage imaging provides 261 a direct and precise representation of electrophysiological events. Recent advances in 262 voltage indicators, such as QuasAr6a 37  and zArchon1 38 , have significantly contributed to 263 enabling imaging speeds up to 1,000 Hz, allowing researchers to resolve fast voltage 264 transients critical for understanding neural dynamics. However, such high-speed imaging 265 significantly reduces photon collection, leading to a low SNR. The resulting noise not only 266

- obscures neuronal morphology but also distorts voltage signals, making it challenging to 267 extract meaningful dynamics. These challenges necessitate robust denoising methods 268 that can preserve both the spatial and temporal fidelity of voltage imaging data. Our  results  show  that  FAST 273 significantly improves both the clarity of neuronal morphology and the fidelity of extracted 274 voltage signals, enabling more accurate analysis of neural activity under extreme imaging 275 conditions. 276

# Discussion 452
Noise presents a significant challenge in intravital neural observation, with inherent shot 453 noise  setting  the  ceiling  for  the  SNR  in  fluorescence  imaging,  thereby  constraining 454 resolution,  speed,  and  sensitivity.  Effective  denoising  is  crucial,  and  different  imaging 455 scenarios  require  tailored  approaches:  structural  imaging  benefits  from  high  spatial 456 resolution, while functional imaging demands high temporal resolution. Self-supervised 457 deep learning methods have emerged as powerful tools for denoising, and leveraging 458 spatiotemporal  redundancy  in  raw  data.  However,  existing  approaches  often  involve 459 complex training and resource-intensive processes, and it remains challenging to provide 460 the fast, high-quality denoising techniques needed for neuroscience research to support 461 real-time  data  analysis  and  closed-loop  neural  modulation.  We  introduce  FAST,  a 462 universal real-time self-supervised denoising pipeline for diverse neural  imaging 463 scenarios. FAST uses a lightweight 2D convolutional network to balance temporal and 464 spatial redundancies, achieving rapid denoising speeds beyond 1,000 FPS, and extreme 465 to  2,100  FPS.  It  has  been  validated  across  various  imaging  scenarios  and  subjects, 466

- demonstrating superior denoising performance and real-time capability. FAST enhances 467 cellular morphology restoration, neuron segmentation, and 3D calcium event extraction 468 while preserving  spike  shapes  and  improving  voltage  transient  correlations  with 469 electrophysiological  recordings.  A  user-friendly  GUI  further  facilitates  training,  offline 470 inference, and real-time online inference, enabling state-of-the-art denoising of user data. 471

Previous denoising methods for fluorescence time-lapse imaging often relied on large472 scale network structures, such as 3D  convolutional networks, Transformers, or 473 combinations of multiple architectures 15,16,21,24 . However, we argue that such complexity 474 is  unnecessary.  FAST,  with  its  spatiotemporal  balanced  training  strategy,  achieves 475 denoising speeds exceeding 1,000 FPS on a single GPU using only a lightweight 2D 476 convolutional network. The performance of FAST meets the real-time denoising demands 477 of most imaging systems, while still leaving time windows available for additional post478 processing operations, such as cluster analysis of large-scale neuronal imaging, real479 time spike inference, functional connectivity analysis, online activity pattern recognition, 480 optogenetic stimulation feedback, and automated ROI selection and tracking 44 -48 . 481

Existing self-supervised time-lapse denoising methods rely on temporal redundancy to 482 recover true signals from noisy data. These methods are based on the assumption that 483 information  carriers  maintain  ergodicity  across  adjacent  temporal  coordinates.  This 484 foundational  assumption,  however,  confronts  inherent  limitations  when  the  temporal 485 sampling rate is low or the signal's dynamics are fast. Hence, in practical ultra -high speed 486 imaging acquisition, such as neuronal voltage imaging, the dynamics between a spike 487 window are too sharp to maintain the assumption after temporal subsampling, and further 488 lead deviations that can lead to distortion and smoothed spatial structure of recovered 489 signals.  Most  current  methods  seek  to  maximize  the  temporal  input  range,  aiming  to 490 enhance denoising performance by capturing potential signal features. However, a wider 491 temporal input range often contains several dynamics. A self-supervised approach relying 492 solely on temporal redundancy would cause a phantasm of temporal causality, wherein 493 signal  restoration  highly  depends  on  future  signals,  especially  in  3D  convolutional 494 networks. This temporal causality phantasm inevitably introduces uncertainties in ultra495 high speed imaging, compromising the authenticity of the restored signal. FAST mitigates 496

- this issue by incorporating adjustable trade-off parameters that constrain the temporal 497 receptive field and expand the spatial receptive field. By tuning the information-receiving 498 range, FAST effectively minimizes interference at its source, preserving the authenticity 499 of neural signals while reducing noise. This controlled approach enables the rapid and 500 faithful  restoration  of  high-fidelity  signals  without  relying  on  extensive  spatiotemporal 501 inputs. 502

Our well-designed frame-multiplexed spatiotemporal learning strategy equips FAST with 503 a universal self-supervised denoising capability, demonstrated to be effective across a 504 wide  range  of  biological  samples,  including  zebrafish  and  mice.  It  is  versatile  in  its 505 application,  supporting  multiple  imaging  modalities  such  as  calcium  imaging,  voltage 506 imaging, and volumetric imaging, as well as various imaging techniques like confocal 507 microscopy,  light-sheet  microscopy,  and  multi-photon  microscopy.  Beyond  this,  we 508 believe FAST has the potential to be implemented in other biomedical optical imaging 509 techniques,  offering  improvements  in  depth,  resolution,  and  speed.  Therefore,  we 510 envision FAST as providing universal ultra-fast denoising integrated with imaging systems 511 and experimental requirements, thereby opening up new possibilities for advanced and 512 verifiable biomedical research. 513

# Network architecture and loss function 535
Network structure: The FAST network is a meticulously designed ultra-lightweight 2D 536 U-Net, as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 3.  Similar to the original U-Net 48 , our network 537 architecture employs an encoder-decoder structure with skip connections.  In our network, 538 we use two encoding blocks to reduce the dimensionality.  Each encoding block consists 539 of a 3×3 group convolutional layer (with each group processing 2 channels) followed by 540 a BatchNorm layer, a ReLU activation, and a 3×3 max-pooling layer.  To restore the input 541 dimensions, we  use two decoding blocks, each containing a nearest-neighbor 542 interpolation, followed by a 3×3 group convolutional layer (with each group processing 2 543 channels), a BatchNorm layer, and a ReLU activation.  Group convolutions reduce the 544 number  of  parameters  and  computational  cost  while  enabling  independent  feature 545 extraction  within  each  group,  which  helps  mitigate  interference  between  groups  and 546 avoids artifacts caused by temporal signal aliasing.  At each resolution depth, the number 547 of channels in each feature map is 64.  We employ skip connections to connect the output 548 of the second encoding block to the input of the corresponding decoding block. 549

Compared to the original U-Net, we have made two principal modifications.  First, we 550 reduced  the  number  of  downsampling  steps  to  two.  Downsampling  increases  the 551 receptive field, allowing the convolutional kernels to extract features over a larger image 552 area.  However, as the number of downsampling steps increases, so does the number of 553 network parameters.  Our spatial subsampler can be regarded as a single downsampling 554

- step  that  expands  the  receptive  field,  thereby  allowing  us  to  reduce  the  number  of 555
- downsampling steps in the U-Net to shrink the network.  Second, we eliminated the top556

level skip connection.  Skip connections can fuse low-level and high-level features, but in

denoising  tasks,  high-level  features  are  often  noise  that  needs  to  be  suppressed.

Therefore, removing the top-level skip connection can improve denoising performance.

- By  minimizing  the  network  depth,  the  number  of  channels  per  feature  map,  and  the 560 number of skip connections, our network trains with only approximately 0.13M parameters. 561

Criteria for publication
Your review is vital in helping our editors decide if the manuscript meets the journal's criteria for publication, and we ask you to keep the following factors in mind when you write your report:
- The quality of the data — whether they are technically sound, obtained with appropriate techniques, analysed and interpreted carefully, and presented in sufficient detail.
- The level of support for the conclusions — whether sufficiently strong evidence is provided for the authors' claims and all appropriate controls have been included.
- The potential significance of the results — whether these results will be important to the field and advance understanding in a way that will move the field forward. (Note that posting of preprints and/or conference proceedings does not compromise novelty.)

The primary purpose of your review is to provide feedback on the soundness of the research reported. This will help authors to improve their manuscript and editors to reach a decision. We do not ask that you make a recommendation regarding publication, but you can set out the arguments for and against publication if you so wish.

Elements of a reviewer report
In your report, please comment on the following aspects of the manuscript.
- Key results: Your overview of the key messages of the study, in your own words, highlighting what you find significant or notable. Usually, this can be summarized in a short paragraph.
- Validity: Your evaluation of the validity and robustness of the data interpretation and conclusions. If you feel there are flaws that prohibit the manuscript's publication, please describe them in detail.
- Significance: Your view on the potential significance of the conclusions for the field and related fields. If you think that other findings in the published literature compromise the manuscript's significance, please provide relevant references.
- Data and methodology: Your assessment of the validity of the approach, the quality of the data, and the quality of presentation. We ask reviewers to assess all data, including those provided as supplementary information. If any aspect of the data is outside the scope of your expertise, please note this in your report or in the comments to the editor. We may, on a case-by-case basis, ask reviewers to check code provided by the authors (see this Nature editorial for more information).
- Analytical approach: Your assessment of the strength of the analytical approach, including the validity and comprehensiveness of any statistical tests. If any aspect of the analytical approach is outside the scope of your expertise, please note this in your report or in the comments to the editor.
- Suggested improvements: Your suggestions for additional experiments or data that could help strengthen the work and make it suitable for publication in the journal. Suggestions should be limited to the present scope of the manuscript; that is, they should only include what can be reasonably addressed in a revision and exclude what would significantly change the scope of the work. The editor will assess all the suggestions received and provide additional guidance to the authors.
- Clarity and context: Your view on the clarity and accessibility of the text, and whether the results have been provided with sufficient context and consideration of previous work. Note that we are not asking for you to comment on language issues such as spelling or grammatical mistakes.
- References: Your view on whether the manuscript references previous literature appropriately.
- Your expertise: Please indicate any particular part of the manuscript, data or analyses that you feel is outside the scope of your expertise, or that you were unable to assess fully.

Providing constructive feedback
We ask reviewers to approach peer review with a sincere intention to help the authors improve their manuscripts. Nearly all submissions have weaknesses to be addressed: the best and most constructive reports suggest specific improvements; such feedback can be used by authors to improve their manuscript to the point where it might be suitable for acceptance. Even in instances where manuscripts are rejected, your report will help authors interpret the editor's decision and improve their work prior to submission elsewhere.
You should be direct in your report, but you should also maintain a respectful tone. As a matter of policy, we do not censor the content of reviewer reports; any comments that were intended for the authors are transmitted, regardless of what we may think of the content. On rare occasions, we may edit a report to remove offensive language or comments that reveal confidential information about other matters.

Now write the full reviewer report in natural flowing prose, as a human expert would. Do not use labeled section headers. Mentally consider all the elements above (validity, significance, methodology, suggested improvements, etc.) but weave them naturally into your writing rather than addressing each as a separate heading.
